analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits for retirees, disabled people, and survivors, funded by payroll taxes on income above $400,000 and investment income.
analysis.headline: The Social Security 2100 Act, which would have raised benefits and applied Social Security taxes to income above $400,000, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in July 2023 and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would expand Social Security for current and future beneficiaries: bigger checks for nearly everyone for a decade, a higher minimum benefit for long-term low earners that climbs up to the poverty level, better benefits for widows and widowers, an annual boost for people who have been on benefits more than 15 years, credit for unpaid caregivers of children and chronically dependent relatives, an end to the five-month waiting period for disability benefits, and repeal of the rules (the "windfall elimination provision" and "government pension offset") that cut benefits for people who also collect government pensions from jobs that didn't pay Social Security taxes. It also would let children of deceased or disabled workers keep benefits through age 25 if they are in school, and stop Social Security field office closures without public hearings. To pay for it, the bill would apply Social Security payroll taxes to wages above $400,000 and for the first time levy the 12.4% Social Security tax on net investment income of high-income households, and it would combine the retirement and disability trust funds into one.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries: everyone would get a temporary across-the-board increase in how benefits are calculated (the first benefit "bend point" rises from 90% to 93% of average earnings for 2025–2034) [S2] [S3]. Long-term low earners would get a guaranteed minimum benefit tied to the federal poverty guideline, scaling up with years worked [S3]. Widows and widowers in two-income households would get larger survivor benefits [S2] [S3]. About two million-plus current and retired public servants — teachers, police, and firefighters with pensions not covered by Social Security — would get their full Social Security benefits back, since the bill repeals the windfall elimination provision and government pension offset for 2025–2034 [S2] [S3]. People on disability would get benefits starting immediately instead of after a five-month wait, and disabled people who work would face a gradual reduction in benefits instead of losing them outright [S3]. Unpaid caregivers of young children or chronically dependent relatives would earn Social Security credit for those years [S3]. Children of deceased or disabled workers could keep benefits through age 25 as students [S2]. Seniors would pay income tax on less of their Social Security income, with the threshold raised to $35,000 single / $50,000 joint [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security beneficiaries and public pensioners

how_it_helps.text: Raises the first benefit calculation factor from 90% to 93% of average indexed monthly earnings, increasing benefits for essentially all beneficiaries for 2025 through 2034.
Creates a minimum benefit for long-term low earners that rises from 6.25% to 125% of the federal poverty guideline depending on years worked, benefiting people with 11 or more years of work.

Repeals the windfall elimination provision and the government pension offset, restoring full Social Security benefits for people who also receive pensions from employment not covered by Social Security, for 2025 through 2034.

Applies Social Security payroll taxes to income above $400,000 and, for the first time, applies the 12.4% Social Security tax to net investment income of higher-income taxpayers, which is the bill's main pay-for.

Eliminates the five-month waiting period before disability benefits begin and replaces the current cliff that terminates benefits for disabled people who return to work with a gradual $1-off-for-every-$2 reduction.
Grants Social Security earning credit (deemed wages) for up to five years spent caring for a dependent child under 12 or a chronically dependent relative, up to half the national average wage.

Uses whichever of the CPI-W or CPI-E (an index tracking typical spending by people 62 and older) is higher to calculate annual cost-of-living increases, which would raise annual COLAs for seniors during 2024 through 2033.
Raises the income thresholds at which Social Security benefits become taxable to $35,000 for singles and $50,000 for joint filers, cutting federal income tax on benefits for middle-income seniors.
Extends child's benefits to full- and half-time post-secondary students up to age 25/26, and eases eligibility for children living with grandparents or other relatives.

Adds an annual increase of up to 5% of a benchmark benefit for beneficiaries 16 or more years after first becoming eligible, targeting long-serving disability and elderly beneficiaries whose benefits erode over time.
Prevents closure of Social Security field and hearing offices without conditions such as public hearings, protecting in-person access to the agency.

analysis.who_pays: The bill is paid for entirely by high earners and wealthy households: wages and self-employment income above $400,000 would be subject to Social Security payroll taxes for the first time (they currently stop counting above a lower annual cap), with an employee-side rule ensuring workers with multiple employers pay only the combined amount; and net investment income of higher-income taxpayers would be subject to the 12.4% Social Security tax on top of the existing 3.8% Medicare tax [S2] [S3]. Employees pay half the payroll tax and employers pay the other half, so high-wage businesses and their executives both bear new costs. Very high earners would also begin accruing small additional Social Security benefits (1% of earnings above $400,000 counts in the benefit formula), though far less than they would pay in [S3]. Many of the benefit increases are temporary: most provisions apply to benefits payable in 2025 through 2034 and then expire [S3].

drawbacks.text: Most of the benefit improvements are temporary: the across-the-board increase, minimum benefit, COLA change, WEP/GPO repeal, caregiver credits, and other provisions apply to benefits payable in calendar years 2025 through 2034 and then sunset, so a beneficiary's higher benefit would be recomputed back down after 2034.

The new payroll tax applies to income above $400,000 at a combined 12.4% split between workers and employers, so high-income workers would see smaller take-home pay and their employers would face higher labor costs, though the bill includes a rule ensuring workers with several employers pay no more than the single-employer amount.

The bill does not raise general revenue to pay for the benefits; the entire cost falls on the highest-earning roughly 0.5% of earners (above the $400,000 threshold) and on investment income of high-income households, which critics would note is a narrow base being asked to fund a broad, though temporary, expansion.

Applying Social Security tax to net investment income at 12.4% on top of the existing 3.8% Medicare surtax would be a large new tax on capital returns for higher-income households, which its opponents characterized as unfair taxation of retirement savings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad, immediate, and targeted at people who have historically been shortchanged: low earners, widows, disabled people facing a five-month wait, and two million-plus public employees whose benefits were cut by the windfall elimination provision. The cost is narrow and falls on income above $400,000 and on high-income investment returns. The main honest criticism is design: nearly all the benefit increases expire after 2034, so the bill delivers a decade of higher checks rather than a permanent higher benefit floor, while the tax structure it creates (taxing income above the cap with only a token 1% benefit accrual) points toward a permanent new levy. As a benefit bill for ordinary people, the trade is favorable; as a permanent fix for Social Security's long-run financing, it is more of a down payment than a settlement.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended without any vote anywhere.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Blumenthal introduced the Social Security 2100 Act on July 12, 2023, joined by four Democratic cosponsors (Sens. Whitehouse, Padilla, Duckworth, and Luján).
The same day it was introduced, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.

No further action was ever taken: the bill received no committee markup, no hearing-related advance on the record, no floor vote, and never left committee before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The Congress has ended, so the bill is dead; any reintroduction would have to start over in a new Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners and wealthy households come out ahead: they will not pay the new Social Security tax on wages above $400,000 or the new tax on net investment income that the bill would have imposed. Social Security beneficiaries and public pensioners, the bill's intended beneficiaries, receive nothing because it never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and investors spared new taxes

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on July 12, 2023.

for.name: Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse, Alex Padilla, Tammy Duckworth, and Ben Ray Luján
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: 4 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's four cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Ron Wyden)
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by a Democrat
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred on July 12, 2023; no markup, no hearing on the bill, no vote, for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None signed on as cosponsors; the bill drew no Republican support at any point.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic — one sponsor and four Democratic cosponsors, none of the 49 Senate Republicans — and even within the Democratic caucus only 4 of 48 members signed on.

industries.note: The bill's pay-fors fall entirely on them: Social Security payroll taxes would apply to wages and self-employment income above $400,000, and the 12.4% Social Security tax would be levied on net investment income of higher-income taxpayers in addition to the existing 3.8% Medicare tax. Because the bill died, they pay nothing.

Payroll taxes are split between employee and employer, so firms paying executives above $400,000 would have owed the 6.2% employer share on that excess income. The bill's death leaves their costs unchanged.

industries.industry: State and local government workers with non-Social Security pensions (teachers, police, firefighters)
industries.note: Repeal of the windfall elimination provision and government pension offset would have restored Social Security benefits these workers earned from other jobs but currently lose or have reduced because of their government pensions. The repeal was temporary (2025–2034) and never happened.
